title: Unique Paths

problem.description:
There is a robot on an m x n grid. The robot is initially located at the top-left corner (i.e., grid[0][0]). The robot tries to move to the bottom-right corner (i.e., grid[m - 1][n - 1]). The robot can only move either down or right at any point in time.

Given the two integers m and n, return the number of possible unique paths that the robot can take to reach the bottom-right corner.

The test cases are generated so that the answer will be less than or equal to 2 * 10^9.

Example 1:

Input: m = 3, n = 7
Output: 28

Example 2:

Input: m = 3, n = 2
Output: 3
Explanation: From the top-left corner, there are a total of 3 ways to reach the bottom-right corner:
1. Right -> Down -> Down
2. Down -> Down -> Right
3. Down -> Right -> Down

Constraints:

- 1 <= m, n <= 100

hints: A robot starts in the top-left cell of an `m × n` grid and may only step right or down. Count how many different routes lead it to the bottom-right cell.

Every cell in the top row, and every cell in the left column, can be reached in exactly one way: a straight line. In Example 2 (`m = 3`, `n = 2`) all three routes contain exactly two Downs and one Right; they differ only in the order of those moves.

With `m, n <= 100` there are at most `10^4` cells, so work proportional to the size of the grid is instant. Following routes one at a time is not: answers go up to `2·10^9`, so enumerating them means billions of steps.

This is grid dynamic programming for counting: the number of ways to reach a cell is the sum of the ways to reach the cells you can enter it from. Because every route is a fixed mix of two kinds of moves, it is also a combinatorics (binomial coefficient) problem.

Every route uses exactly `m - 1` Downs and `n - 1` Rights, so a route is decided by choosing which of its `m + n - 2` moves are Downs. The answer is therefore the binomial coefficient `C(m + n - 2, m - 1)`.

Build `C(N, k)` with `N = m + n - 2` and `k = min(m, n) - 1` as a running value `res` that starts at `1`: at step `i` it is multiplied by `N - k + i` and then divided by `i`, after which it equals `C(N - k + i, i)`. Keep `res` in a 64-bit integer because the product before the division can exceed `2^31`.

Set `N = m + n - 2` and `k = min(m, n) - 1`.
Set a 64-bit `res = 1`.
For `i` from `1` to `k`:
multiply `res` by `N - k + i`,
then divide `res` by `i` (always exact).
Return `res`.

The trickiest step is keeping every intermediate exact and in range: multiply before dividing (each partial result is a whole binomial coefficient), use 64-bit because a product can reach about `2.8·10^10`, and never compute full factorials like `198!`. When `m = 1` or `n = 1`, `k = 0`, the loop does nothing, and the answer is `1`. Time is `O(min(m, n))` and extra space is `O(1)`.

normal.note: Small square grid: 2 Downs and 2 Rights in any order, `C(4, 2) = 6`.
Example 1 transposed: swapping `m` and `n` must not change the count.
Medium square grid where plain recursion already repeats a lot of work: `C(18, 9) = 48620`.
Larger rectangle with a nine-digit answer, `C(33, 11)`.

edge.note: Single cell: the start is the target, and the empty route counts as one path.
Single row at maximum width: only Right moves, so exactly one path.
Single column at maximum height: only Down moves, so exactly one path.
Two rows: the single Down can happen in any of the 100 columns.
Tall narrow grid at maximum height: `C(101, 2) = 5050`.
Near the `2·10^9` cap: `C(33, 16)`; the last product before dividing overflows a 32-bit `int`.
Maximum height with the widest grid that stays under the cap: `C(105, 6)`.

approach.oneLiner: Count the distinct sequences of Down and Right moves that take the robot from cell `(0, 0)` to cell `(m - 1, n - 1)` of an `m × n` grid.
approach.pattern: Grid DP for counting paths, which collapses to a binomial coefficient
signals: "The robot can only move either down or right" → a cell can be entered only from the cell above or the cell on its left, so `ways(i, j) = ways(i - 1, j) + ways(i, j - 1)`: grid DP.
"return the number of possible unique paths" → a counting question (add the counts of the choices), not a max/min optimisation.
"the answer will be less than or equal to 2 * 10^9" → the result fits in a 32-bit `int`, but a formula's intermediate products may not, and visiting paths one by one would take billions of steps.
"1 <= m, n <= 100" → at most `10^4` cells, so an `O(m·n)` table is tiny and even simpler closed forms are worth looking for.
approach.constraints: `m, n <= 100` means at most `10^4` cells, so an `O(m·n)` DP is about `10^4` additions and a closed formula needs at most `99` multiply/divide steps. Plain recursion makes `2 × answer - 1` calls, about `2.3·10^9` for `m = 17, n = 18`, far too slow. So any polynomial method is fine; the target is `O(m·n)` or better.

thinking.q: How can I count paths without listing them?
thinking.a: Look at the last move into the target `(m - 1, n - 1)`: it came either from the cell above or from the cell on the left, and those two groups never overlap. So `paths(i, j) = paths(i - 1, j) + paths(i, j - 1)`, with every top-row and left-column cell reachable in exactly one way.

thinking.q: Why is recursing on that formula slow even for small grids?
thinking.a: The same cell is counted from many parents: in a `3 × 3` grid `paths(1,1)` is solved once for `paths(1,2)` and again for `paths(2,1)`. Each leaf adds just `1`, so the recursion makes about `2 × answer` calls, billions when the answer is near `2·10^9`.

thinking.q: In what order can I compute each cell exactly once?
thinking.a: A cell needs only the cell above and the cell to its left, so filling the grid row by row, left to right, always has both ready. That is `m·n <= 10^4` additions, and `dp[m - 1][n - 1]` is the answer (for Example 1, `28`).

thinking.q: What do all the paths in Example 2 (`m = 3`, `n = 2`) have in common?
thinking.a: Each has exactly two Downs and one Right: `Right→Down→Down`, `Down→Down→Right` and `Down→Right→Down` differ only in where the single Right sits. In general every path has `m - 1` Downs and `n - 1` Rights.

thinking.q: So is there a closed form?
thinking.a: A path is fixed once you choose which of its `m + n - 2` moves are Downs, so the count is `C(m + n - 2, m - 1)`. For Example 1 that is `C(8, 2) = 28`, matching the table.

thinking.q: How do I evaluate `C(N, k)` without overflow or fractions?
thinking.a: Take `k = min(m, n) - 1` and build `res = res × (N - k + i) / i` for `i = 1..k` in 64-bit. After each step `res` equals `C(N - k + i, i)`, a whole number, so the division is exact, and no product exceeds about `2.8·10^10`.

approaches.name: Recursion on the last move
approaches.aha: Asking 'where did the robot come from just before this cell?' gives the recurrence immediately, and recursing on it is the first thing anyone writes.
approaches.idea: Let `paths(i, j)` be the number of Down/Right paths from `(0,0)` to `(i, j)`. If `i = 0` or `j = 0` the cell is on the top row or left column and only one straight path reaches it. Otherwise the last move was a Down from `(i - 1, j)` or a Right from `(i, j - 1)`; those groups are disjoint and together contain every path, so `paths(i, j) = paths(i - 1, j) + paths(i, j - 1)`. The answer is `paths(m - 1, n - 1)`, but since every leaf contributes only `1`, the work grows with the answer itself.
steps: Otherwise compute `up = paths(i - 1, j)` and `left = paths(i, j - 1)`.
approaches.complexity: Every base case returns `1`, so the call tree has exactly `answer` leaves and `answer - 1` inner calls: `2·C(m + n - 2, m - 1) - 1` calls, exponential in `m + n`. The only extra memory is the recursion stack, at most `m + n - 2` frames, because each call lowers `i + j` by one.
approaches.tradeoff: The same cell is recomputed from many parents (`paths(1,1)` twice even in `3 × 3`), so a grid like `17 × 18` needs about `2.3·10^9` calls and times out.

pseudocode: function uniquePaths(m, n)
ans ← paths(m - 1, n - 1)  // count the paths that end in the bottom-right cell
return ans
function paths(i, j)  // number of Down/Right paths from (0,0) to cell (i, j)
if i = 0 or j = 0
return 1  // top row or left column: only a straight line reaches it
up ← paths(i - 1, j)  // paths whose last move is Down, from (i-1, j)
left ← paths(i, j - 1)  // paths whose last move is Right, from (i, j-1)
total ← up + left  // the two groups share no path, so add them
return total

parts.why: Every leaf returns 1 and the root adds them all up, so there are exactly `answer` leaves.
Each inner call makes exactly two calls, and a full binary tree with `answer` leaves has `answer − 1` inner nodes.

time.sum: answer + (answer − 1) = 2·C(m + n − 2, m − 1) − 1 calls of O(1) work; since C(N, k) ≤ 2^N, this is O(2^(m + n)).
time.cases: A single row or column (`m = 1` or `n = 1`) makes just one call; for a fixed `m + n`, square grids are the worst because the middle binomial coefficient is the largest.
time.feel: m = 3, n = 7 → 55 calls; m = 17, n = 18 → about 2.3·10^9 calls, several seconds in C++, so it times out.

parts.cost: at most m + n − 2 frames × O(1)
parts.why: Each call lowers i + j by one, and the recursion stops as soon as i or j reaches 0.

space.sum: Only one chain of calls is alive at a time, so the peak is O(m + n) frames of O(1) each.
space.note: No table is stored; the grid itself is never built.

steps.explain: uniquePaths(3, 3) calls paths(2,2) for the target cell; i = 2 and j = 2 are both non-zero, so it must recurse.
paths(2,2) asks paths(1,2) for its up value, which in turn asks paths(0,2); (0,2) is on the top row, so it returns 1.
Back in paths(1,2): up = paths(0,2) = 1.
paths(1,2) now asks paths(1,1), which gets up = paths(0,1) = 1 and left = paths(1,0) = 1 and returns total = 2.
paths(1,2): left = paths(1,1) = 2.
paths(1,2): total = up + left = 1 + 2 = 3, which it returns as the up value of paths(2,2).
Back in paths(2,2): up = paths(1,2) = 3.
paths(2,2) now asks paths(2,1) for its left value; i = 2 and j = 1 are both non-zero, so it recurses.
paths(2,1) asks paths(1,1) — the same cell already solved two steps earlier — and it redoes paths(0,1) and paths(1,0) to return 2 again. This repeated work is what makes the recursion exponential.
Back in paths(2,1): up = paths(1,1) = 2.
paths(2,0) is in the left column, so it returns 1.
paths(2,1): left = paths(2,0) = 1, so total = 2 + 1 = 3, which it returns.
Back in paths(2,2): left = paths(2,1) = 3.
paths(2,2): total = up + left = 3 + 3 = 6, and it returns 6.
The outer call paths(2,2) has returned, so ans = 6.
Return ans = 6.

dryRun.result: 6 — the target (2,2) is reached by 3 paths through (1,2) plus 3 paths through (2,1); C(4, 2) = 6 confirms it.

approaches.name: 2D DP table filled row by row
approaches.aha: The recursion solves the same cell again and again (`paths(1,1)` twice even in `3 × 3`), yet there are only `m·n` distinct cells; storing each count once, in an order where the cell above and the cell on the left are already known, removes all the repetition.
approaches.idea: Let `dp[i][j]` be the number of paths from `(0,0)` to `(i, j)`. Every cell in row `0` or column `0` gets `1`, because only a straight line reaches it. Any other cell is entered by a Down from `(i - 1, j)` or a Right from `(i, j - 1)`, and those two groups never overlap, so `dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] + dp[i][j - 1]`. Filling rows top to bottom and each row left to right guarantees both neighbours are final when they are read, so `dp[m - 1][n - 1]` is the answer.
steps: Set every cell in row `0` and column `0` to `1`.
For `i` from `1` to `m - 1` and `j` from `1` to `n - 1`, set `dp[i][j] = dp[i - 1][j] + dp[i][j - 1]`.
approaches.complexity: The double loop visits each of the `m·n` cells exactly once and does one addition, so at most `10^4` operations. The `dp` table holding all `m·n` counts is the extra memory.
approaches.tradeoff: It passes the limits easily, but it keeps all `m·n` counts although each row only reads the row above (one rolling row of `n` cells would give `O(n)` space), and it still does `m·n` additions where a closed formula needs only `min(m, n) - 1` steps.

pseudocode: function uniquePaths(m, n)
dp ← m × n table of 0  // dp[i][j] = number of paths from (0,0) to (i, j)
for i ← 0 to m - 1
for j ← 0 to n - 1
if i = 0 or j = 0
dp[i][j] ← 1  // first row or first column: one straight path
else
up ← dp[i - 1][j]  // paths arriving by a Down move
left ← dp[i][j - 1]  // paths arriving by a Right move
dp[i][j] ← up + left  // the two groups are disjoint, so add
return dp[m - 1][n - 1]

parts.why: Zero-filling the table touches every cell once.
Each cell is set to 1 or to one addition of two already-known cells.

time.feel: m = n = 100 → 10^4 cells and about 2·10^4 simple operations, a few microseconds.

parts.why: One path count per cell of the grid.

space.sum: m·n integers = O(m·n); at most 10^4 ints, about 40 KB.
space.note: Keeping only the previous row would cut this to O(n) with the same recurrence; the inputs and the returned int are not counted.

steps.explain: Create a 3 × 3 table of zeros; dp[i][j] will hold the number of paths into cell (i, j).
Cell (0,0) is the start cell, reachable by a single straight path, so dp[0][0] = 1.
Cell (0,1) is in the first row, reachable by a single straight path, so dp[0][1] = 1.
Cell (0,2) is in the first row, reachable by a single straight path, so dp[0][2] = 1.
Cell (1,0) is in the first column, reachable by a single straight path, so dp[1][0] = 1.
Cell (2,0) is in the first column, reachable by a single straight path, so dp[2][0] = 1.
Return dp[2][2] = 6.

dryRun.result: 6 — dp[2][2] = dp[1][2] + dp[2][1] = 3 + 3, and the table is Pascal's triangle, so the corner equals C(4, 2) = 6.

approaches.name: Binomial coefficient C(m + n − 2, m − 1)
approaches.aha: Every entry of the `dp` table counts arrangements of Downs and Rights — `dp[i][j] = C(i + j, i)`, Pascal's triangle — so the bottom-right entry is one binomial coefficient and the table is not needed at all.
approaches.idea: A path is fully described by which of its `N = m + n - 2` moves are Downs, and any choice of `m - 1` positions gives a valid path, so the count is `C(N, m - 1) = C(N, n - 1)`. Using `k = min(m, n) - 1` keeps the loop as short as possible. Building it as `res = res × (N - k + i) / i` for `i = 1..k` keeps every intermediate equal to the whole number `C(N - k + i, i)`, so integer division never loses anything, and a 64-bit `res` absorbs the temporary product before each division.
steps: Set `N = m + n - 2` and `k = min(m, n) - 1`.
For `i` from `1` to `k`, multiply `res` by `N - k + i`.
Then divide `res` by `i`; the result is exactly `C(N - k + i, i)`.
approaches.complexity: The loop runs `k = min(m, n) - 1 <= 99` times with one multiplication and one division each, so time is `O(min(m, n))`. Only a few scalars (`N`, `k`, `res`, `i`) are stored, so extra space is `O(1)`.
approaches.tradeoff: With at most `99` arithmetic steps and constant memory there is nothing meaningful left to save. The trade-off is generality: the formula works only because every cell is open, so blocked cells (Unique Paths II) or weighted cells send you back to the DP.

pseudocode: function uniquePaths(m, n)
N ← m + n - 2  // total moves on every path
downs ← m - 1  // every path has exactly m-1 Down moves ...
rights ← n - 1  // ... and exactly n-1 Right moves
k ← min(downs, rights)  // C(N, downs) = C(N, rights); the smaller k means fewer steps
res ← 1  // 64-bit; after step i it holds C(N - k + i, i)
for i ← 1 to k
res ← res × (N - k + i)  // multiply first ...
res ← res / i  // ... then divide: the result is a whole binomial, so this is exact
return res  // C(N, k): ways to place the k rarer moves among N slots

parts.why: A few additions, one min and one assignment.
One multiplication and one exact division per iteration.

time.cases: `m = 1` or `n = 1` gives k = 0, so the loop never runs and the answer is 1; otherwise the length depends only on the smaller side.
time.feel: At most 99 iterations for any allowed input; Example 1 (m = 3, n = 7) needs just 2.

parts.part: Scalars N, downs, rights, k, res, i (lines 2-7)
parts.why: No table and no recursion are used.

space.sum: 6 scalars regardless of m and n = O(1).
space.note: `res` must be 64-bit: the product before a division can exceed 2^31 − 1 (up to about 2.8·10^10) even though the final answer fits in an int.

steps.explain: N = m + n - 2 = 3 + 7 - 2 = 8: every path makes exactly 8 moves.
downs = m - 1 = 2: every path goes down exactly 2 times.
rights = n - 1 = 6: every path goes right exactly 6 times.
k = min(2, 6) = 2: choosing where the 2 Down moves go among 8 slots fixes the path, and the smaller k means only 2 loop steps.
res = 1, the empty product (C(anything, 0) = 1).
res = 7 / 1 = 7, which is exactly C(7, 1).
res = 56 / 2 = 28, which is exactly C(8, 2).
The loop is done; return res = 28 = C(8, 2).

dryRun.result: 28 — choosing which 2 of the 8 moves are Downs gives C(8, 2) = 28, the same as filling the 3 × 7 table.

mistakes: Computing `C(m + n - 2, m - 1)` from full factorials: `198!` overflows every integer type long before the division; build the value incrementally instead.
Dividing before multiplying, or keeping `res` in a 32-bit `int`: `res / i` on its own is not always a whole number, and `res × (N - k + i)` can reach about `2.8·10^10`, overflowing `int`.
Off-by-one moves: a path has `m - 1` Downs and `n - 1` Rights, not `m` and `n`; using `C(m + n, m)` gives `C(10, 3) = 120` instead of `28` for Example 1.
Starting the DP with only `dp[0][0] = 1` and then reading `dp[i - 1][j]` and `dp[i][j - 1]` for every cell without handling row `0` and column `0`, which reads outside the table.
edgeCases: `m = 1, n = 1`: the start is the target, so the answer is `1` (the empty path); `k = 0` and the loop never runs.
`m = 1` or `n = 1` (for example `1 × 100`): only one straight path exists, so the answer is `1`, not `0` or `100`.
`m = 2, n = 100`: the answer is `100`, one path for each column where the single Down can happen; it checks that `k = min(m, n) - 1 = 1` is used.
`m = 17, n = 18`: the answer `1166803110` is close to the `2·10^9` cap and the last product `565722720 × 33` exceeds `2^31`, catching a 32-bit `res`.

related.title: Unique Paths II
related.why: The same grid DP with blocked cells; the closed formula no longer works, so the table (or one rolling row) is required.

related.title: Minimum Path Sum
related.why: The same right/down grid recurrence, but taking the minimum of the two neighbours plus the cell cost instead of adding counts.

related.title: Climbing Stairs
related.why: The 1D version of counting ways: `ways(i) = ways(i - 1) + ways(i - 2)`, summing over the possible last moves.

related.title: Pascal's Triangle
related.why: Each entry is the sum of the two above it, which is this problem's table rotated 45 degrees; its entries are the binomial coefficients used in the formula.

takeaways: To count paths in a grid where moves only go forward, `ways(cell)` is the sum of `ways` over the cells that can step into it; fill the table in an order where those cells come first.
When every valid object is an arrangement of a fixed multiset of moves, the count is a binomial coefficient, so check for a formula before building a table.
Compute `C(N, k)` incrementally with `res = res × (N - k + i) / i` in 64-bit, using the smaller of `k` and `N - k`; every intermediate is a whole number, so the division is exact.
